title: Not one sparrow (Luke 12:1–12)
hook: five sparrows sold for two pennies, and none forgotten; your hairs are numbered

segments.voice: Yesterday, a cup clean on the outside, and a God who made the inside too. Your line was the inside too. What quiet, generous thing did you do? Day five hundred forty-seven.

Luke says the crowd had grown so big that people were treading on one another. Thousands, pressing in. And Jesus turns first to his own friends and talks about fear. Not the crowd's fear, theirs. Fear of being found out, fear of powerful people, fear of standing up in front of judges one day and not knowing what to say. It's a heavy start. And then, to make his point, he reaches for the smallest, cheapest thing in the marketplace: a little brown bird, sold by the handful for food.

In the King James Bible: "Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings, and not one of them is forgotten before God?" A farthing was the smallest English coin the translators knew. In the Greek it's an assarion, a little Roman copper coin, a fraction of a day's wage. Sparrows were poor people's meat, sold in bunches. Now here's the detail people love once they spot it. In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus says two sparrows are sold for one farthing. In Luke, five for two. Do the arithmetic. Pay for four, and the seller throws in a fifth for free. The bird that isn't even worth a price. And that's the one Jesus says God hasn't forgotten. Then he comes closer: "But even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not therefore: ye are of more value than many sparrows." Numbered. Not loved in general, as a crowd, but known down to a detail you don't even know about yourself. That's the ground under everything else he says in this passage. Don't fear those who can only kill the body. Say openly who you belong to. And when you're dragged before authorities, don't rehearse a speech, because, as he puts it, "the Holy Ghost shall teach you in the same hour what ye ought to say." For Luke's first readers, some of whom would really stand before judges, those weren't abstract words. Courage, in this passage, doesn't come from being tough. It comes from being known. If even the free sparrow isn't forgotten, neither are you.
screen: then, large: `NOT ONE OF THEM IS FORGOTTEN BEFORE GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, in two parts. Today, if you can, put out a few crumbs or seeds for the birds, or just stop and watch some, the small ordinary ones nobody photographs. For now, settle and breathe. Think of the thing you're most afraid of this week. Hold it for a moment. Then picture the fifth sparrow, the one thrown in for free, and the line that not one of them is forgotten. If you pray, you can place your fear next to that sparrow. If you don't, simply notice that the fear is held, and so are you. The bell holds the time.
Not one sparrow. Five little birds sold for two coins, the fifth one free, and not one of them forgotten before God.
Your line: not one forgotten. Today, notice the person in the room most easily overlooked, and let them know you've seen them. Day five hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Christians often turn to this passage in times of fear or grief, and it lies behind the old hymn His Eye Is on the Sparrow; Francis of Assisi is remembered for preaching to the birds.

fork.setup: you're at a market in Galilee. sparrows are two for one coin. you hand over two coins. how many birds do you get?
fork.reveal: Matthew says two for a farthing; Luke says five for two. the fifth is thrown in free, and not one of them is forgotten before God.

original.note: Greek, borrowed from Latin: a small copper coin. the King James Bible says farthing.

trapdoor: what you thought: God cares about birds, so God cares about people.
what it means: even the cheapest bird is remembered, and people are known down to the hairs of their heads, so they need not fear.
what a scholar hears: Matthew's two-for-one and Luke's five-for-two suggest the fifth sparrow was thrown in for nothing, and that is the one not forgotten.

notes: The 'fifth sparrow free' reading of Matthew 10:29 vs Luke 12:6 is a common preacher's and commentator's observation; it is inference, not stated in the text. Consider softening if a Keeper prefers.
Sparrows as cheap food sold in markets: standard background. Confirm.
Assarion value ('a fraction of a day's wage'): roughly 1/16 of a denarius. Confirm.
His Eye Is on the Sparrow (1905) draws on Matthew 10:29–31 as much as Luke; howItsDone keeps it general.
